labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

items.body:
## Summary

An existing image-heavy Codex desktop chat repeatedly becomes unusable: even a short continuation remains running without assistant output, retries WebSocket connections, and falls back to an HTTP request that also stalls. Rebooting and forking the chat did not recover it.

**Final controlled result:** the remote WebSocket path accepts a 16,773,121-byte uncompressed JSON message and returns `OK` / `response.completed` in 4.714 seconds, but rejects a 16,781,313-byte message with an actual received **Close 1009** in 1.802 seconds. Both contain the same 26 decoded images and write only about 36 KB to the socket after compression. This brackets the remote message-size boundary within an 8 KiB interval around **16 MiB** and separates it from slow-upload/heartbeat effects. The affected desktop request is approximately 19.57 MB, above this measured boundary, while its token estimate remains below automatic compaction.

A controlled synthetic test now reproduces a specific transport failure. The same 26 images, with identical decoded pixels and dimensions, complete in 3.3 seconds when encoded in a small request. Padding the PNGs to approximately the affected history's byte size causes the upload to remain unfinished until the server closes the WebSocket with **1011, `keepalive ping timeout`**. The send callback then reports `write EPIPE`.

This establishes a reproducible payload-size-dependent heartbeat failure on this network path. It does not yet establish which network component slows or blocks the upload, a universal request-size limit, or that every reported reconnect has this cause.

**Further control:** sending the byte-identical large message in 64 KiB WebSocket fragments kept heartbeats working for more than five minutes, but ultimately received **Close 1009 (message too big)** before inference began. Fragmentation therefore exposes a second failure and is **not a complete fix** for this large request. The precise configured size limit has not been established.

## Environment

- Codex desktop app `26.1013.40934`; bundled CLI `0.163.0-alpha.10.2`.
- macOS `26.6.2 (25G83)`, Apple Silicon.
- Model `gpt-6-astra`, desktop reasoning effort `xhigh`, built-in OpenAI provider, ChatGPT sign-in.
- A local proxy/VPN is active. Reconnecting it and changing the proxy node did not recover the desktop chat. Network contribution remains under investigation.
- Tests below were performed on 2026-10-20, Asia/Shanghai (UTC+08:00).

## Controlled reproduction

The probes use the standard Responses WebSocket protocol and the same authenticated OpenAI destination as Codex. They are separate Node.js probes, **not an instrumented build of the bundled Rust client**. Credentials remain local; only synthetic image data is sent. Both small and large probes use the same prompt, model, image count, decoded pixels and dimensions. The controls use `gpt-6-astra`, reasoning effort `low`, reasoning summary `concise`, image `detail: low`, and no tools. The original desktop turn uses `xhigh`; the probes isolate transport bytes rather than recreating its entire semantic context.

Each large PNG contains a valid private ancillary `npAD` chunk with random bytes. This changes encoded request size without changing the decoded image. The payloads contain no original document text, screenshots or personal image pixels.

| Measurement | Small control | Large control |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Number of images | 26 | 26 |
| Total PNG bytes | 241,224 | 14,092,925 |
| Base64 characters | 321,668 | 18,790,596 |
| Full JSON request bytes | 324,045 | 18,792,973 |
| WebSocket upgrade | HTTP 101 | HTTP 101 |
| Extension | permessage-deflate | permessage-deflate |
| Send callback | Success, 3 ms after open | `write EPIPE`, about 83.1 s after open |
| Model result | `OK`, `response.completed`, 3.30 s total | No `response.created` or model output |
| Close | Normal completion | **1011: `keepalive ping timeout`**, 85.14 s total |

The large probe received a server Ping at 22.644 s, while its initial request was still uploading. The send callback never completed successfully before the close. Small-control input usage was 5,796 tokens.

Redacted large-probe event sequence (milliseconds since probe start):

```jsonl
{"type":"starting","elapsed_ms":99,"request_bytes":18792973}
{"type":"upgrade","elapsed_ms":2030,"status":101,"extension":"permessage-deflate"}
{"type":"open","elapsed_ms":2032}
{"type":"ping","elapsed_ms":22644}
{"type":"send_callback","elapsed_ms":85133,"error":"write EPIPE"}
{"type":"close","elapsed_ms":85136,"code":1011,"reason":"keepalive ping timeout"}
```

## Affected desktop chat

The original chat's logged connections repeatedly fail approximately 80–82 seconds after a successful handshake: measured intervals include 82.100, 82.035, 82.001, 82.035 and 80.015 seconds. Errors include:

```text
stream disconnected before completion: IO error: Broken pipe (os error 32)
websocket closed by server before response.completed
```

The app retries full requests with `reason=connection_closed`, reaches 5/5 retries, then falls back to HTTP. One logged HTTP body measured `pre_compression_bytes=19568737`, `post_compression_bytes=12438883` (zstd). After the reboot at 23:58 on October 19, the chat was continued at 00:00 on October 20 and still produced no assistant/tool output during the investigation. A separate diagnostic chat in the same app/account/model/network works.

A read-only audit reconstructed 232 active history items totaling approximately 19,453,560 serialized UTF-8 bytes. There are 26 distinct, valid inline images with 18,791,180 data-URL characters, about 96.6% of the active history size. Strict base64 and full pixel decoding pass; no duplicate item IDs, unmatched tool call/output pairs or invalid history-base byte boundaries were found.

The last logged active-context estimate was 222,686 tokens, below the 244,800 automatic-compaction threshold and 258,400 context limit; both context-limit flags were false. The cumulative database token counter is not being used as the active-context estimate.

A similarly sized HTTP request from the original chat previously received HTTP 200. Consequently, this report does **not** claim that requests of this size always fail or that a hard size cap has been established. A later status read confirmed that the last affected desktop turn ended as interrupted at 00:11:57, after approximately 713 seconds with no assistant/tool output. It was not still running during the synthetic controls below.

## Additional route and HTTP controls

Bypassing the explicit local HTTP CONNECT proxy while retaining the system VPN/TUN route reproduced the same large-request failure. The WebSocket opened at 0.756 s. At 20.755 s the server Ping caused an automatic Pong to be queued; the Pong callback did not return until 83.769 s, with `EPIPE` — a queue delay of 63.014 seconds. The data send also failed, and the server closed with 1011, `keepalive ping timeout`, at 83.771 s. This rules out a problem unique to the explicit local proxy port; it does not rule out the common VPN/upstream route.

A zstd-compressed HTTP control of the same large image payload produced a 13,873,772-byte compressed body. It returned no HTTP status or model event within the probe's 150-second diagnostic deadline. The probe then aborted it. The abort is not evidence that the server rejected the request, and a callback triggered during teardown is not counted as successful upload completion.

## Fragmentation exposes a second failure: Close 1009

The TUN single-frame control and fragmented controls use the exact same 18,792,973-byte JSON body, SHA-256 `d048183c4603cb4166e2de4d3fbe0a440a9801323b2e45e63c61842580420661`, same destination, model, compression negotiation and system route. Only WebSocket framing and the probe deadline changed. The fragmented sender uses 64 KiB fragments, waits for each send callback, and yields the event loop before sending the next fragment so control frames can be processed.

An initial fragmented run was deliberately aborted at its 300-second diagnostic deadline while heartbeats were still working. A second run used a longer deadline and reached a distinct server close:

- Ten server Ping/automatic-Pong cycles succeeded; the largest local Pong-write callback delay was approximately 3.24 seconds. These are local write-completion timings, not end-to-end server receipt measurements.
- At 318.308 seconds, the client had completed send callbacks for 16,777,216 JSON characters (16 MiB; this synthetic JSON is ASCII).
- While attempting the next fragments, the socket entered CLOSING. The callback reported that state at 331.571 seconds, with the sender's offset at 17,432,576. This offset is **not** a server-confirmed delivered-byte count.
- At 334.584 seconds, the close event recorded **1009**, with an empty reason. No `response.created` or `response.completed` was received.

[RFC 6455 section 7.4.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455.html#section-7.4.1) defines 1009 as a message too large to process. This initial observation suggested a limit near 16 MiB; the subsequent narrow boundary control below tests that inference directly.

## Completed intermediate-size control

A 9,437,185-byte JSON request (9 MiB + 1 byte), using the same 26 decoded images with shorter random PNG padding and the same TUN/64 KiB-fragment route, successfully completed despite the slow upload:

- Successful final local send callback: 210.619 seconds.
- `response.created`: 229.161 seconds.
- `response.completed`, output `OK`: 230.929 seconds.
- Input usage: **5,796 tokens**, identical to the small control.

This confirms that the fragmented path can actually finish a slow, larger-than-trivial request; surviving heartbeats alone is not being treated as successful inference.

## Fast boundary test isolates decoded message bytes

To remove slow upload as a confound, two further groups use **all-zero** valid `npAD` chunks. They preserve the same 26 decoded images and use the same model, prompt, options, TUN route, compression and 64 KiB framing. Zero padding makes the encoded JSON highly compressible, while preserving its uncompressed size. CRC checks and full pixel equality pass for every image pair.

| Measurement | Below boundary | Above boundary |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Actual JSON bytes | **16,773,121** | **16,781,313** |
| Relative to 16 MiB | −4,095 bytes | +4,097 bytes |
| PNG bytes, total | 12,578,058 | 12,584,202 |
| Successful local send callback | 1.069 s | 0.940 s |
| Socket bytes written at send callback | 36,047 | 36,113 |
| First `response.created` | 3.057 s | None |
| Outcome | **`OK`, `response.completed` at 4.714 s** | **Raw received Close frame 1009 at 1.802 s** |
| Input tokens | 5,796 | No inference response |

The above-boundary probe recorded the raw receiver `conclude` event, code 1009 and empty reason, before the connection close event. Neither probe emitted a local `ws` maxPayload / `WS_ERR_UNSUPPORTED_MESSAGE_LENGTH` error. This distinguishes a received remote Close from the Node client's own receive-size enforcement. `socket.bytesWritten` is a local counter, not a packet capture including TLS overhead; nevertheless, both writes are small and both complete well before any heartbeat timeout.

The observed acceptance/rejection bounds are **16,773,121 to 16,781,313 uncompressed JSON bytes**. This strongly supports a remote decoded-message limit around 16 MiB on this authenticated WebSocket route. It does not establish the exact configured integer, which backend/edge component enforces it, an HTTP limit, or a universal limit for other endpoints.

For reproduction, use the same PNG construction below with zero padding instead of random padding. For a desired JSON byte target `T`, this exact request scaffold has 2,377 bytes of fixed JSON/data-URL overhead. Set total raw PNG bytes to `(T - 2377) / 4 * 3`, distribute the total across 26 files in multiples of three bytes, and insert `bytes(desired_png_size - len(small_png) - 12)` in the `npAD` chunk. Targets 16,773,121 and 16,781,313 yield the totals in the table. Serialize compact ASCII JSON and verify the actual size before sending; different prompts or fields change the fixed overhead.

## Client diagnostics and requested investigation

Please investigate heartbeat handling while a large initial request is still being transmitted, including backpressure and proxy interactions. The public release tag matching the installed CLI version, `rust-v0.163.0-alpha.10.2`, resolves to commit `4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4`. Its socket pump waits inside the send branch and cannot poll its read/Ping branch until that send resolves:

- [Single pump: awaited send at line 80; Ping/Pong in the alternate read branch at lines 94–95](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/codex-api/src/endpoint/responses_websocket.rs#L70).
- [The request is sent as one Text message](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/codex-api/src/endpoint/responses_websocket.rs#L1000).
- [The release's pinned Tungstenite implementation turns Text into a single final frame, without automatic fragmentation](https://github.com/openai-oss-forks/tungstenite-rs/blob/4fffad30fe373adbdcffab9545e9e9bf4f2fc19f/src/protocol/mod.rs#L571).
- [The Close code and reason are discarded](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/4ebc485ca321243727539187169425fcf972f2c4/codex-rs/codex-api/src/endpoint/responses_websocket.rs#L945).

These observations are from the matching public release tag; a reproducible-build comparison with the installed binary has not been performed. The Node probe is a separate client. It has automatic Pong enabled, but the Pong write queues behind the large unfinished frame. The synthetic probe supplies the explicit close reason that the desktop log does not retain. The source and probe together support a heartbeat-starvation mechanism under upload backpressure, rather than proving the exact source of that backpressure.

Useful fixes to investigate include checking decoded message bytes before sending, enforcing a byte-aware history/image budget separately from token-based compaction, keeping control frames responsive during slow uploads, retaining Close code/reason, and providing a supported recovery action for affected chats. Fragmentation alone does not bypass the message-size limit. Retrying the same oversized full history cannot resolve that size rejection, and generic reconnect errors leave the user unable to tell that inference has not begun.

Related reports: #51889 and #52456. The similarity alone does not prove a shared cause.

## Privacy

This public report contains only reviewed measurements, synthetic test details and redacted errors. No original screenshots, document contents, private prompts, raw rollouts, credentials, account identifiers, thread/turn identifiers or local personal paths are included. The described controls are complete; their terminal outcomes are distinguished from deliberately aborted probes. No original conversation history or system network settings were modified.

## Synthetic fixture generator

Run this standalone script with `uv run generate.py --out /your/test/directory`. It reads no source images and performs no network requests. Pass the generated PNG bytes verbatim as `input_image` data URLs; a UI that re-encodes the PNGs may strip the padding and invalidate the size comparison.

<details>
<summary>Self-contained generator, with CRC and decoded-pixel checks</summary>

```python
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10"
# dependencies = ["pillow==13.0.0"]
# ///
"""Generate synthetic PNG pairs differing only in transport bytes; no network calls."""
import argparse
import base64
import hashlib
import io
import json
from pathlib import Path
import random
import struct
import zlib
from PIL import Image

# width, height, padded file size in bytes. No source images are read.
PROFILE = [
 (1980,1280,670397),(1976,1248,508080),(921,2048,144508),(1220,319,63394),
 (2048,1169,404103),(2048,1169,321886),(1810,1280,386573),(1280,1814,528395),
 (1279,1801,487338),(1814,1280,475457),(1279,1798,349442),(1800,1279,314879),
 (1279,1792,277412),(1801,1279,393905),(953,1348,119913),(953,1348,219960),
 (953,1348,224727),(953,1348,274606),(1376,1780,961370),(1376,1780,953521),
 (1376,1780,1023720),(1376,1780,954546),(1516,1072,843429),
 (1334,1888,794600),(1334,1888,1219375),(1334,1888,1177389),
]

def validate_png(raw):
    assert raw[:8] == b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n'
    offset = 8
    while offset < len(raw):
        n = struct.unpack('>I', raw[offset:offset+4])[0]
        kind = raw[offset+4:offset+8]
        content = raw[offset+8:offset+8+n]
        crc = struct.unpack('>I', raw[offset+8+n:offset+12+n])[0]
        assert zlib.crc32(kind + content) & 0xffffffff == crc
        offset += n + 12
    assert offset == len(raw) and kind == b'IEND'
    Image.open(io.BytesIO(raw)).verify()
    decoded = Image.open(io.BytesIO(raw)); decoded.load()
    return decoded

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument('--out', type=Path, default=Path(__file__).parent/'fixtures')
    out = parser.parse_args().out.resolve()
    for group in ('small', 'large'):
        (out/group).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    rng = random.Random(20261020)
    rows = []
    for i, (width, height, target) in enumerate(PROFILE):
        image = Image.new('RGB', (width,height), (30+i*7%200,100+i*5%150,130+i*3%100))
        buffer = io.BytesIO(); image.save(buffer, format='PNG'); small = buffer.getvalue()
        size = target - len(small) - 12
        assert size > 0
        padding = rng.randbytes(size)
        kind = b'npAD'  # ancillary, private, reserved bit valid, unsafe-to-copy
        chunk = struct.pack('>I',size) + kind + padding + struct.pack('>I', zlib.crc32(kind+padding)&0xffffffff)
        large = small[:-12] + chunk + small[-12:]  # insert immediately before IEND
        a, b = validate_png(small), validate_png(large)
        assert a.size == b.size and a.mode == b.mode and a.tobytes() == b.tobytes()
        assert len(large) == target
        row = {'index':i+1, 'width':width, 'height':height, 'pixels_identical':True}
        for group, raw in [('small',small),('large',large)]:
            relative = f'{group}/{i+1:02}.png'; (out/relative).write_bytes(raw)
            row[group] = {'file':relative,'bytes':len(raw),
                          'data_url_chars':22+4*((len(raw)+2)//3),
                          'sha256':hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest()}
        rows.append(row)
    summary = {'image_pairs':len(rows),'all_pairs_pixels_identical':True,
               'png_crc_and_full_decode_verified':True,
               'contains_private_content':False,'model_requests_performed':False}
    for group in ('small','large'):
        summary[group] = {key:sum(row[group][key] for row in rows)
                          for key in ('bytes','data_url_chars')}
    (out/'manifest.json').write_text(json.dumps({'summary':summary,'images':rows},indent=2)+'\n')
    print(json.dumps(summary,indent=2))

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
```

</details>

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Installed Windows package `OpenAI.Codex`: **26.1013.4894.0** (collected locally; not copied from the About dialog).
Bundled Code Review plugin: **26.1013.40934**.

### What subscription do you have?

Not recorded. This occurred in a signed-in ChatGPT-authenticated Codex desktop session.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows x64. PowerShell reports `Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0`.

### What issue are you seeing?

Starting a private PR review fails before a pinned snapshot is returned or a reviewer starts:

```text
GitHub provider request failed (HTTP 502)
```

Two normal `record_private_review(action: "begin")` attempts failed. Read-only diagnostics isolated the failure to:

```text
POST https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/wham/github/operations/review-comparison
diff: true
```

The affected comparison contains **518 changed files, 59,004 additions and 8,312 deletions**. Direct authenticated GitHub access successfully returned its complete raw diff: **52,415,888 bytes**. The Codex provider repeatedly returned an HTTP 502 HTML “Bad gateway” page for the same pinned comparison.

The repository is private. Its name, URL, commit IDs, source contents and local paths are intentionally omitted from this public report.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed on one private PR; a standalone public reproduction has not been established:

1. Open the affected PR in the desktop Code Review workflow using the selected GitHub account.
2. Request a private review and invoke `record_private_review` with `action: "begin"`.
3. Observe the error above instead of a review snapshot.
4. Retry: the same initialization failure occurs.

Additional read-only probes used the bundled provider client and its normal authorization flow, without modifying the installed plugin. The same authenticated GitHub identity was verified for provider and direct GitHub access. Base, merge-base and head were pinned before the comparison checks.

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Provider account and PR metadata | HTTP 200 |
| Provider comparison for the pinned base/head, `diff: false` | HTTP 200 |
| Provider comparison for those same revisions, `diff: true` | Repeated HTTP 502, approximately 3.2–3.8 seconds |
| Direct GitHub compare endpoint, same revisions, `Accept: application/vnd.github.diff` | HTTP 200; complete 52,415,888-byte response |
| Provider comparison using the head's immediate parent as base, same repository and head | HTTP 200; this smaller nonempty comparison's direct raw diff is 7,763,710 bytes |

The complete direct diff was structurally checked: 518 file headers, 59,004 added lines and 8,312 deleted lines matched PR metadata. This was a completeness check, not a review of the application code.

### What is the expected behavior?

Private review initialization should retrieve and verify the complete pinned comparison, or explain a supported size limit and recovery action. It should not silently truncate coverage or reduce a reproducible failure to a generic HTTP 502.

### Additional information

The evidence points to a failure while the Codex GitHub provider handles this large comparison: metadata and a smaller nonempty comparison work, and upstream GitHub can deliver the full diff. **The exact server-side cause is unconfirmed.** These observations do not establish a particular size threshold, memory failure or timeout.

Correlation details from a failing provider probe:

- UTC start: `2026-10-19T16:04:36.466Z`
- Duration: `3227 ms`
- HTTP status: `502`
- Content type: `text/html; charset=UTF-8`
- Server: `cloudflare`
- CF-Ray: `a4d105079a7ef1f4-KHH`
- Error body: `5650 bytes`, HTML “Bad gateway”
- Successful direct GitHub request ID: `AD5A:2D036B:28D0DA:411096:6AD64084`

The client surfaces only the generic provider error when this response is HTML. Preserving a sanitized request identifier and actionable failure reason would help diagnosis.

A separate GitHub PR-diff endpoint rejected the >300-file PR with HTTP 406, but the exact **compare** endpoint returned all 518 files. That separate 406 is not evidence of the cause of this provider 502.

A possible remediation is bounded or streamed diff transport with complete pinned-revision coverage checks. Per-file patch retrieval would need explicit handling of missing or truncated patches.

Related: #49628 and #49565 concern PR discovery/detail loading failures. Here account, PR metadata and comparison metadata all succeed; the failure is specifically the large full comparison during private review initialization. I did not find an existing report with this combination of observations.

No GitHub Actions workflow was invoked. No application code or installed plugin was modified, and no review findings were produced. No credentials, IP addresses, private source files or session archives are attached.

During an active voice conversation in an existing Codex desktop task, the assistant repeatedly read a Spanish message draft aloud after explicit requests to display it only in the chat. ## Observed sequence

This is a report of repeated occurrences in one live session, not a claim of a deterministic reproduction in a clean session.

1. Request a short Spanish message draft and explicitly require written delivery in the chat, without reading it aloud.
2. The assistant starts speaking the draft.
3. Correct it and ask that the preference be saved.
4. The assistant acknowledges written-only delivery, but on subsequent draft turns again speaks the Spanish content.
5. A written inline chat item is produced by the task; the following voice transcript still contains a spoken rendering of the draft, and the user reports the unwanted reading.
6. The preference is saved in local agent instructions. Subsequent user feedback reports another recurrence; that file edit did not establish a working audio-level fix.
7. Later, paste a message already sent and begin explaining a request for an addition. The assistant starts reciting/reworking the pasted message before the user finishes the instruction.

## Short examples from the conversation

Recipient names and the subject matter of the draft are intentionally omitted.

- User: "Just write me the text correctly in the chat ready to paste in WhatsApp."
  - Subsequent voice output recited the proposed draft.
- User: "In this case, I want you to put the message in the chat, not to speak it to me."
  - Assistant described the message as being only in chat, then continued into the Spanish draft aloud.
- User: "You are reading once again."
  - The same complaint recurred after acknowledgements of the preference.
- In a later turn, the user explained that the pasted message had already been sent and began requesting an addition. The assistant began reading the pasted draft while that request was unfinished.

- An explicit request for written-only delivery should produce visible copyable text without reciting, translating or paraphrasing it aloud.
- Written-only delivery should remain distinct from ordinary conversational answers during the same voice call.

Documentation / supported integration clarification; feature request only where no supported interface exists.

### What is the issue?

For Codex Desktop on native Windows, how can a downstream native process controller obtain a supported, version-bound capability describing its actual launch containment and descendant lifetime?

The observed command interface supplies command options, output and a session identifier. Those values alone do not establish the original OS containment objects, their generations, policy stability or a complete descendant-completion boundary. This is an interface limitation in the examined workflow, not evidence that isolation is absent, a security vulnerability, or a universal Windows limitation.

The Windows sandbox documentation describes MXC and legacy implementations, and says remaining MXC child processes stop when the foreground command exits. Please distinguish that documented behavior from the evidence available to a native consumer for a particular invocation. A fixed Windows Job topology should not be presumed across implementations.

### Requested supported contract

Please identify the owning component, applicable Desktop/runtime versions and API/schema, or state explicitly which guarantees are unsupported.

1. Read-only identification of the effective sandbox implementation and permissions for an invocation, rather than inferring them from an app version or a successful shell command.
2. A trustworthy binding between the invocation, original process identities/generations, containment scope and permitted descendant-creation paths, including any breakaway exceptions.
3. Protection lifetime, inheritance, revocation and policy-change semantics. If internal objects remain opaque, an equivalent versioned platform-owned capability is sufficient; exposing every internal handle is not a requirement.
4. Normal exit, cancellation, client interruption, transport loss and sandbox shutdown: what is stopped, when completion is confirmed, and whether bounded cooperative shutdown is compatible with the platform policy. Forced termination must remain distinguishable from cooperative completion.
5. A consumer-verifiable terminal record identifying the covered processes, normal/forced/unknown outcome, any surviving owned descendants and the lifetime of observation resources. Please distinguish attested guarantees from best-effort observations.
6. Reconciliation of an ambiguous result without launching the same effect again. If original handles are exposed, document provenance, minimal rights, transfer and protection lifetime; query access alone is not a temporal guarantee, and retaining handles must not defeat last-handle termination policies.

A documented composition of interfaces is acceptable. This does not request a security bypass, global permission change or privileged process control.

### Scope boundaries

Process exit/output closure is distinct from completion of application-internal callbacks, destructors or service users. This request does not ask OpenAI to certify those internals. ### What variant of Codex are you using?

Cross-variant feature request. This proposal is not tied to a specific client or verified build.

### What feature would you like to see?

Please strengthen the underlying LLM's ML/research capabilities and provide a reusable, LLM-assisted framework that makes it easy for a user to build, evaluate, and iteratively improve their own domain-specific models.

**Problem and motivation**

In my experience, assistance with supervised learning, reinforcement learning, evaluation code, and research-paper-to-implementation work is not yet reliable enough for end-to-end model development. Codex can become stuck repeatedly finding errors or counterexamples while losing sight of the overall functional goal. I want stronger creative problem-solving: propose workable alternatives, implement them, test them, and carry the task through to a useful result.

This matters beyond ML too. Whether building a game, a website, or a business system, local criticism should help complete the intended system. Finding a problem should lead to a concrete fix or a tested alternative, rather than another cycle of criticism.

**Requested workflow**

1. **Turn an idea or paper into a runnable baseline.** Help clarify the objective, read and cite relevant research, identify assumptions, and translate the method into working training and evaluation code. Distinguish established findings from hypotheses that still need testing.
2. **Make setup approachable.** Guide or automate environment setup, dependencies, data preparation, dataset validation, model selection, and training configuration. Support supervised learning and reinforcement-learning workflows without requiring users to assemble all the infrastructure themselves.
3. **Keep the actual goal visible.** Preserve user-defined acceptance criteria throughout debugging and experimentation. Prioritize issues by their impact on the goal, avoid repeatedly reopening resolved concerns without new evidence, and implement constructive fixes when authorized.
4. **Evaluate real progress.** Use suitable baselines and held-out evaluation, guard against leakage, and report uncertainty and relevant trade-offs. For RL, check reward design and whether measured gains reflect the intended behavior. Passing a script or increasing a training metric alone should not count as success.
5. **Support a user-controlled improvement loop.** Diagnose failures, propose changes to data, code, model configuration, or training strategy, run approved experiments, compare results, and retain or roll back changes based on evidence. Let users set compute/time budgets, approval points, and stopping criteria.
6. **Deliver reproducible artifacts.** Keep versioned configurations, data references, seeds, checkpoints, experiment results, and clear instructions to reproduce and use the resulting model.

**Desired outcome**

A user should be able to describe a domain problem and get a working model-development project: a runnable baseline, valid evaluation, practical debugging, and an understandable path to further improvement. The LLM should actively help build and improve that project, rather than stop at advice or lists of possible flaws.

### Additional information

By “self-improving,” I mean iterative improvement of the user's model and development workflow under user-defined goals, permissions, and resource limits. Improvements should be measured and reviewable, with no assumption that every experiment will succeed.

This is a product/capability proposal based on my experience, not a controlled bug reproduction or a claim about an internal training cause.

Related: #4293 discusses feedback-driven optimization of the assistant itself. This request focuses on helping users create and improve their own domain-specific models, with stronger end-to-end ML implementation and research support.

The Responses API proxy could reuse a federated credential after an upstream `401`, and concurrent requests could each retry a failed token exchange.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Installed Windows package inspected: `OpenAI.Codex_26.1013.4894.0_x64`. This is the package version, not a value copied from the About dialog.

### What subscription do you have?

Not included in this report.

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0 x64.

### What issue are you seeing?

Desktop worktree creation no longer respects the Git configuration used for a separate Codex SSH identity when refreshing upstream. This workflow previously worked; the last known good version and introducing release have not yet been identified. The reporter's macOS setup still works, but its configuration has not been compared, so this is not proof that the underlying code path is Windows-only.

The global Codex `config.toml` defines `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` and `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL` under `[shell_environment_policy.set]`. Both are correctly present in agent-run commands. The selected Git config includes an HTTPS-to-SSH URL rewrite. Ordinary Git inspection in the agent environment resolves the repository's origin to SSH.

During desktop-managed worktree creation, the upstream-refresh fetch instead uses HTTPS and fails authentication. Sanitized log evidence from 2026-10-19 12:53:08 UTC:

```text
requestKind=create-worktree source=worktree_pending_create
subcommand=fetch exitCode=128 success=false
[worktree-create] upstream-refresh-failed branchName=main remote=origin
error: unable to read askpass response from '<Git installation>/mingw64/bin/git-askpass.exe'
fatal: could not read Password for 'https://<redacted>': terminal prompts disabled
```

The same attempt subsequently logs `[worktree-create] ready`. The refresh failure can therefore result in a worktree based on cached Git state, rather than preventing all worktree creation.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Use a private GitHub repository whose stored origin URL is HTTPS.
2. Configure an HTTPS-to-SSH rewrite in the global Git configuration used by Codex:

```gitconfig
[url "git@github.com:"]
    insteadOf = https://github.com/
```

3. Keep a separate SSH identity for Codex, selected through global Codex configuration, using paths appropriate to the machine:

```toml
[shell_environment_policy.set]
GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL = 'C:/path/to/codex.gitconfig'
GIT_SSH_COMMAND = 'C:/Windows/System32/OpenSSH/ssh.exe -F NUL -o IdentityFile=none -i C:/path/to/codex-key -o IdentitiesOnly=yes'
```

4. Confirm that agent commands receive both variables and `git remote get-url origin` resolves to SSH.
5. Create a desktop-managed worktree from a branch with an upstream. Inspect the upstream-refresh log: the fetch uses HTTPS and attempts password authentication instead.

A read-only diagnostic reproduced the transport difference without creating a worktree or changing repository configuration: `git remote get-url origin` resolves to SSH with the normal Codex environment, but resolves to HTTPS after applying the desktop refresh's global/system Git config isolation.

### What is the expected behavior?

Desktop-managed Git operations, including the pre-worktree upstream refresh, need a supported app-wide way to use the user's explicitly configured Codex Git authentication and URL-routing settings.

The Codex identity must remain confined to Codex. Requiring Windows user-wide Git environment variables would also affect unrelated terminals and Git clients. Repeating SSH configuration in every repository is not an acceptable replacement for the previously working central configuration.

Please preserve the relevant trusted authentication and URL-resolution settings when isolating Git configuration, or provide a supported Codex-scoped configuration surface that the desktop worker actually consumes. This is not a request to remove all Git isolation or change the user's personal Git identity.

### Additional information

Read-only inspection of the installed desktop bundle found that the upstream-refresh path:

- Reads the configured `remote.<name>.url`.
- Runs fetch with `GIT_CONFIG=NUL`, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=NUL`, `GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1`, and `GIT_PROTOCOL_FROM_USER=0` on Windows.
- Copies only `credential.*` settings from global/system configuration into command-line overrides.

This excludes the global `url.*.insteadOf` rewrite and `core.sshCommand`, and explicitly supersedes the selected `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL`. An SSH command cannot select an SSH key for a fetch that is still using HTTPS. The inspected code uses `/dev/null` instead of `NUL` on non-Windows platforms, so the isolation itself appears cross-platform.

The observed loss of URL rewriting is confirmed; the desktop worker's complete process environment and whether it receives `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` were not directly measured. Agent-command environment propagation should not be confused with desktop-worker propagation.

A temporary read-only check showed that Git's runtime `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`/`GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0`/`GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0` URL rewrite survives this file isolation. However, supplying these through an app-specific launcher has not been tested end-to-end and should not be necessary to retain centrally configured Codex authentication.

Suggested regression coverage: a private HTTPS origin with a trusted Codex-scoped SSH rewrite and dedicated identity should refresh successfully during worktree creation, while unrelated desktop Git clients retain the user's personal identity.

### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI (`codex exec`), 0.163.0

### What feature would you like to see?

A client-side check that ends a streamed reply once it has clearly turned into a repetition loop, instead of reading it to the model's output limit.

**What happens today.** The main turn request carries no output cap (`ResponsesApiRequest` in `codex-rs` has no `max_output_tokens` field), and I couldn't find a mid-stream repetition check. I pointed `codex exec` at a local Responses endpoint that streams one sentence on repeat, about 300,000 characters. Codex read all of it and printed all 300,049 characters to stdout:

```sh
export LOOP_KEY=dummy
codex exec --skip-git-repo-check \
  -c 'model_providers.loop={name="loop",base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8765/v1",wire_api="responses",env_key="LOOP_KEY"}' \
  -c model_provider=loop -m loop-model "hello" < /dev/null > out.txt
wc -c out.txt   # 300049
```

The endpoint and runner are here: https://github.com/simin-yuan/agent-runaway-bench

**Why it matters for `codex exec`.** Nobody is watching to press Ctrl-C. In CI or a scheduled job the loop goes into the log or the next step, and the turn runs until the model's own limit. Repeating and degenerate output has been reported here recently (#40957, where the app streamed repetitive garbage tokens into the output, and #40369), so this isn't only a synthetic case.

**A possible approach.** Hermes Agent does this on its chat-completions and Anthropic streams (`RunawayStreamWatch`, NousResearch/hermes-agent#130551): it watches the streamed text, and once a long stretch is dominated by verbatim copies of a few lines, it closes the stream and ends the turn with a clear message. It only fires on long repetition (tens of thousands of characters), so a reply where the user asked for repetition, or a table with similar rows, still comes through. Two details that came up when I wired the same check into two more of Hermes's streams (NousResearch/hermes-agent#141479): skip any drain of the remaining stream after the cut, and drop a tool call that was cut halfway, so the next request doesn't carry a call without a result.

### Additional information

- This measures the client only. I didn't test whether the hosted Responses API stops a looping generation on its side; if it does, the cost side of this is smaller, though `codex exec` would still print the loop up to that point.
- Measured at `openai/codex` main `89461ea` and the 0.163.0 npm release, Ubuntu 24.04.
- Same test against other frameworks, for comparison: Hermes stops at about 16,000 characters; OpenAI Agents SDK 0.24.0, smolagents 1.26.0 and LangGraph 1.2.16 read the whole stream.

items.title: Fall back when macOS rejects high stdio descriptors
items.body:
Fall back when macOS rejects high stdio descriptors

## Why

On macOS, spawn file actions reject valid descriptors at or above `OPEN_MAX` even when `RLIMIT_NOFILE` permits them. This can prevent child processes from starting when their stdio descriptors exceed that limit.

## What changed

Use the compatibility backend when `posix_spawn_file_actions_adddup2` returns `EBADF` for stdio setup and `SpawnFallback::Compatible` is enabled. Preserve the error for `SpawnFallback::ReturnError`.

## Testing

Add a macOS regression test that forces high stdio descriptors and checks strict-mode errors, fallback stdio and exit status, process groups, and descriptor isolation without changing the parent's descriptor.

I am experiencing a serious issue with Codex CLI where my 5-hour usage quota appears to decrease rapidly **before I even submit a single prompt**.

### Observed behavior

I launched Codex CLI and started composing my prompt. While I was still typing and had not pressed Enter to submit anything, Codex displayed multiple usage warnings in succession:

- "Heads up, you have less than 50% of your 5h limit left."
- "Heads up, you have less than 25% of your 5h limit left."
- "Heads up, you have less than 10% of your 5h limit left."

**I had not submitted any new prompt, received any model response, or intentionally initiated any agent task during this period.**

The warnings appeared while I was still composing my input. I was effectively losing access to my usage allowance before I could even start working.

### Why this is concerning

This is not simply a case of high token consumption from a complex task. The unexpected quota changes occurred without any new user-submitted prompt.

I cannot determine whether this represents actual background model requests, delayed accounting from previous sessions, or an incorrect usage display.

Regardless of the underlying cause, there was no visible activity explaining the apparent quota depletion.

### Impact

This significantly disrupts the usability of Codex CLI. A substantial portion of the 5-hour allowance appeared to disappear without any new user-requested work.

### Request

Could the Codex team investigate:

1. Whether any background model requests are being triggered while the CLI is idle or while the user is composing a prompt.
2. Whether completed or previously interrupted sessions could be consuming additional quota.
3. Whether delayed usage accounting or incorrect synchronization could explain the successive warnings.
4. Whether the backend usage records show actual model requests corresponding to these quota changes.

The attached screenshot shows the 50%, 25%, and 10% usage warnings appearing in succession.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Launch Codex CLI in a terminal while authenticated with a ChatGPT Plus account.
2. Open a Codex session.
3. Start typing a new prompt, but **do not press Enter or submit it**.
4. Leave the prompt composer open without intentionally triggering any agent tasks.
5. Observe the usage-limit notifications.

**Actual result:** During the affected session, Codex displayed warnings indicating that less than 50%, then 25%, then 10% of the 5-hour usage limit remained, even though no new prompt had been submitted.

The issue may be intermittent. I have not yet identified a reliable trigger.

### What is the expected behavior?

Codex CLI should not consume additional usage quota merely because a session is open or a user is typing an unsubmitted prompt.

If the remaining quota decreases because of previously completed requests or delayed backend accounting, this should be clearly distinguishable from new usage.

In particular:

- No new model requests should be triggered simply by editing an unsubmitted prompt.
- The usage indicator should accurately reflect actual billable usage.
- Any significant quota decrease should be traceable to identifiable model requests or usage-accounting adjustments.

The 5-hour quota should not appear to drop rapidly without any corresponding visible activity or explanation.

The attached screenshot was captured from Codex CLI and shows the following warnings:

Please add an action in Settings to review and clean up **temporary working files created by Codex during tasks**.

### User need

During local work, Codex can create temporary test scripts, fixtures, scratch directories, and intermediate outputs in `/tmp`, the operating system's temporary directory, or other temporary working locations. Users want to reclaim the space these files use after the relevant tasks finish.

The documented Settings do not describe a cleanup control specifically for these agent-created files, and users cannot easily determine which temporary files belong to Codex or are safe to remove.

### Requested behavior

- Make Codex-created temporary working files discoverable, with their location and disk usage.
- Provide a cleanup action for disposable files from completed tasks, ideally selectable by chat or task.
- Protect files still needed by running tasks and files belonging to other applications. Never indiscriminately empty a shared temporary directory.
- Preserve project source, tests intended to stay in the project, saved deliverables, chat history, credentials, and settings.

Desktop environment: macOS, app version **26.1013.40934**, build **20770**.

Codex **Cloud** has become unusable from my iPad. Two distinct errors appear depending on the client:

1. **Safari / ChatGPT Codex web:** `Error submitting message — Can't find variable: DisposableStack`, shown immediately when attempting to submit a prompt.
2. **ChatGPT iOS app / Codex Cloud:** `Codex server returned an error`, shown immediately after sending a short read-only prompt or pressing **Retry** on an existing cloud conversation.

I can view the conversation history, but I cannot reliably continue the existing Cloud task. **This is Codex Cloud, not a Codex CLI/desktop Remote Control session.** The two errors may have separate root causes.

## Environment

- Device: iPad
- OS: **iPadOS 26.7.1**
- Web client: Safari at `chatgpt.com`, Codex Cloud
- Alternative client: ChatGPT app, Codex Cloud
- Subscription: ChatGPT Plus; Codex usage limits were not exhausted
- Models tried: GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Luna (changing model did not resolve it)
- First observed: **October 19, 2026**

## Steps to reproduce

**Web client**

1. Open an existing, long-running Codex Cloud conversation in Safari on iPad.
2. Enter a short read-only request (e.g. `Report Git status only; do not change files.`).
3. Submit it.
4. Observe an immediate red submission error: `Can't find variable: DisposableStack`. The prompt does not proceed to normal task execution.

**ChatGPT app**

1. Open the same existing Codex Cloud conversation in the ChatGPT app.
2. Submit a short read-only request or tap **Retry**.
3. Observe `Codex server returned an error` immediately, without visible task execution.

## Expected behavior

Both clients should accept new prompts and resume the existing Cloud task, preserving its repository working tree and any uncommitted changes. If a cloud session cannot be resumed, the UI should provide an actionable diagnostic and a safe recovery route.

## Actual behavior / impact

- New prompts cannot be submitted/processed.
- An existing, substantial Cloud development task is blocked.
- The affected task may contain **uncommitted changes**; there is no verified off-environment copy of the most recent edits.
- The UI does not identify whether the Cloud workspace/session is preserved or recoverable.

## Troubleshooting already completed

- Tested **two different networks** (Wi-Fi and mobile hotspot): same failure.
- No VPN enabled.
- Changed model family: same error.
- Codex usage limits were available, not exhausted.
- Both web and ChatGPT app surfaces were tried.

## Engineering questions

1. Is the Codex web bundle using `DisposableStack` without a compatibility fallback/polyfill for the affected Safari runtime? Please investigate; this is a hypothesis, **not a confirmed root cause**.
2. Is the separate immediate Cloud server error caused by task/session resumption or workspace state?
3. Can the affected existing workspace and **uncommitted changes** be preserved/recovered?
4. Is there a supported iPad-only workaround that does not discard or recreate the original session?

I can provide screenshots, account/session identifiers and additional diagnostics **privately** through a secure support channel. I am deliberately omitting private repository information, account identifiers, URLs for the affected task and screenshots with personal browser content from this public report.

### Related but not identical

Reports about mobile Remote Control show a similar generic server error (e.g. #37967 and #44110), but this report concerns **ChatGPT Codex Cloud**, not a CLI session attached from a mobile device.

items.title: Honor per-thread unload delays in app-server
items.body:
Honor per-thread unload delays in app-server

## Why

Thread unload timing used the server-wide delay, ignoring per-thread configuration overrides. Clients need to control how long individual idle, unsubscribed threads remain loaded.

## What changed

- Resolve unload timing from each loaded thread's `thread_unload_delay_secs` configuration. Setting it to `0` allows immediate unloading once the thread has no subscribers or activity.
- Allow this runtime retention override in `experimentalPredictionMode` forks while continuing to reject other configuration overrides. Reject negative values and delays too large to schedule.
- Replace the source-specific immediate-unload behavior with explicit configuration.

## Testing

Extend integration coverage for per-thread delays, unloading after active turns finish, fork overrides, and invalid prediction-fork delays. Verify that immediate unloading preserves persistent history and that cold resumes and ordinary nested forks use their default delay instead of retaining the previous runtime's override.

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI — codex-cli 0.159.2 (`codex exec` / app-server), Windows 11, PowerShell 7.6.6 as the session shell. The code path below is unchanged on `main` as of 2026-10-19.

### What feature would you like to see?

A way to run **command hooks on Windows without wrapping them in the session's PowerShell**.

Today every command hook inherits the session shell: `build_hooks_config` (`codex-rs/core/src/session/mod.rs`) derives the hook shell from `environment.shell` via `derive_exec_args`, so with the default Windows shell each hook runs as

```
pwsh.exe -NoProfile -Command "<hook command>"
```

Observed process chain for a `PreToolUse` hook: `codex.exe → pwsh.exe → bash.exe`.

PowerShell startup/teardown dominates the hook latency:

| Measurement (PreToolUse hook, same payload) | p50 |
|---|---|
| End-to-end inside Codex (pwsh process start → exit) | 3.4 s (2.0–5.2) |
| pwsh start → hook script start | 2.2 s |
| The hook script itself (bash) | 0.55 s |
| Hook script exit → pwsh exit | 0.38 s |
| Empty `pwsh -NoProfile -Command "exit 0"`, idle machine | 1.2 s |

Measured with 4 Codex tasks running concurrently; on an idle machine the absolute numbers roughly halve, the ratio stays (~85% of the hook time is PowerShell, ~15% is the hook). Because `PreToolUse` blocks every tool call, this adds roughly 1–2.5 minutes to a typical task (21–49 tool calls per task across our last 170 tasks). Setting `POWERSHELL_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT=1` / `POWERSHELL_UPDATECHECK=Off` made no measurable difference.

Any one of these would solve it:

1. **An argv / exec form** for command hooks, spawned directly without a shell, e.g. `"command": ["bash", "C:/path/to/hook.sh"]`.
2. **A `shell` setting** per hook (or for all hooks), e.g. `"shell": "cmd"` or `"shell": "none"`.
3. **On Windows, use `COMSPEC /C` for hooks** instead of the session shell — `build_command` / `default_shell_program` in `codex-rs/hooks/src/engine/command_runner.rs` already implement this path when `shell.program` is empty.

### Additional information

- The hook schema (`HookHandlerConfig::Command`: `command`, `commandWindows`, `timeout`, `async`, `statusMessage`, `additionalContextLimit`) has no way to choose the launcher; `commandWindows` only changes the command string, which still goes through pwsh.
- The same hook script started directly (without pwsh) takes ~0.3 s on this machine.
- Process chain captured with `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process`. Timings come from process `StartTime` / `ExitTime` (handles opened while the processes were alive), not from `logs_2.sqlite` timestamps, which are delivery times and can lag behind the real events.

Extend integration coverage for cached subagent hooks under both startup readiness modes, startup timeouts without context injection, and namespace attribution for hook and token-budget context while keeping tools hidden from the model. items.body:
### What version of the IDE extension are you using?

26.527.31454

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Plus

### Which IDE are you using?

VS Code

### What platform is your computer?

Ubuntu Linux (x64)

### What issue are you seeing?

## Summary

An outdated Codex VS Code extension on Ubuntu Linux repeatedly returned HTTP 400 errors indicating that several models were unsupported when using a ChatGPT account.

The errors persisted across multiple model selections and configuration changes, making the problem appear related to authentication, account entitlements, or model availability.

**The issue was resolved immediately after manually updating the Codex VS Code extension.**

I subsequently discovered that automatic updates had been disabled for the extension, although I do not know why.

The main issue is that **Codex provided no warning that the installed extension was outdated or that updating it might resolve the errors**.

This appears closely related to #54422 and #53865, but affects the VS Code extension on Linux rather than the Windows desktop app.

## Environment

| Component | Version / Details |
|---|---|
| OS | Ubuntu Linux (x64) |
| IDE | Visual Studio Code 1.137.0 |
| Extension | OpenAI Codex (`openai.chatgpt`) |
| Extension version before update | Likely `26.527.31454` (see note below) |
| Extension version after update | `26.1007.21434` |
| Subscription | ChatGPT Plus |
| Authentication | ChatGPT account |
| Standalone Codex CLI | `0.114.0` (during troubleshooting) |
| Date resolved | October 19, 2026 |

### Previous extension version

After updating, I inspected the local VS Code extension directories:

```bash
ls -d ~/.vscode/extensions/openai.chatgpt-*
```

Output:

```text
openai.chatgpt-26.1007.21434-linux-x64
openai.chatgpt-26.527.31454-linux-x64
```

The older `26.527.31454` directory is still present, suggesting this was the previously installed version.

However, I did not record the active extension version before updating, so I cannot definitively confirm that this was the version responsible for the issue.

## Observed behavior

While using Codex in VS Code, requests repeatedly failed with HTTP 400 errors.

Example:

```json
{
  "type": "error",
  "status": 400,
  "error": {
    "type": "invalid_request_error",
    "message": "The 'gpt-5.5' model is not supported when using Codex with a ChatGPT account."
  }
}
```

Similar errors occurred when attempting to use:

- `gpt-5.2`
- `gpt-5.5`
- `gpt-6-sol`
- `gpt-6.1-sol`

Removing the explicitly configured model did not resolve the issue either.

The error messages suggested that the selected models were unavailable through ChatGPT authentication.

**At no point did Codex indicate that the extension might be outdated or recommend checking for updates.**

## Troubleshooting performed

Before identifying the solution, I attempted the following:

1. Changed models using the Codex model selector.
2. Explicitly configured different models in `~/.codex/config.toml`.
3. Removed the `model` setting entirely to allow Codex to select its default.
4. Removed `model_reasoning_effort`.
5. Confirmed authentication using:

   ```bash
   codex login status
   ```

   Output:

   ```text
   Logged in using ChatGPT
   ```

6. Checked the standalone CLI version:

   ```bash
   codex --version
   ```

   Output:

   ```text
   codex-cli 0.114.0
   ```

None of the configuration changes resolved the problem inside VS Code.

### Additional CLI diagnostics

During troubleshooting, I also tested the standalone CLI:

```bash
codex exec -m gpt-5.6-terra "Reply with exactly: OK"
```

This produced a different, more informative error:

```text
The 'gpt-5.6-terra' model requires a newer version of Codex.
Please upgrade to the latest app or CLI and try again.
```

The standalone CLI also failed to parse the newer model catalogue because it did not recognize the `max` reasoning-effort value:

```text
unknown variant `max`,
expected one of `none`, `minimal`, `low`,
`medium`, `high`, `xhigh`
```

These diagnostics indicate that my **standalone CLI was also outdated**.

However, the CLI and VS Code extension are separate components. I cannot establish that the standalone CLI caused the original VS Code issue.

The confirmed solution for the IDE was updating the extension.

## Root cause and resolution

I eventually discovered that **automatic updates were disabled for the Codex VS Code extension**.

As a result, I had continued using an outdated extension without realizing it.

I manually updated the extension through VS Code.

**After updating to `26.1007.21434`, Codex started working normally again.**

The issue was therefore resolved without requiring changes to my ChatGPT subscription or authentication method.

The precise reason automatic updates were disabled remains unknown.

## Expected behavior

When an installed Codex extension becomes incompatible with currently available models, I would expect:

1. **Outdated client detection**

   Codex should detect when the installed extension is too old to support the available models.

2. **Actionable error messages**

   Instead of displaying only:

   > The 'gpt-5.5' model is not supported when using Codex with a ChatGPT account.

   The error should distinguish between model availability, account entitlement, and client compatibility problems.

3. **Update notifications**

   The extension should display a warning when an update is required for continued functionality, even if automatic updates are disabled.

4. **Model picker compatibility**

   Models that require a newer client should either be unavailable in the model picker with an explanation or accompanied by an explicit update warning.

5. **Clear recovery instructions**

   Users should be directed to update the VS Code extension rather than repeatedly changing models or authentication settings when client incompatibility is suspected.


## Conclusion

**Status: Resolved locally by updating the VS Code extension.**

I am reporting this because the misleading error messages and absence of actionable update guidance led to unnecessary troubleshooting.

The underlying client compatibility problem may be expected when models evolve, but the user experience could be significantly improved by explicitly identifying outdated extensions and suggesting the appropriate recovery steps.

Hopefully, this report helps other users encountering the same issue.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

## Steps to reproduce

The following is a reconstruction based on my experience. I have not independently reproduced the problem after updating.

1. Install an outdated Codex VS Code extension.
2. Disable automatic updates for the extension.
3. Authenticate using a ChatGPT account.
4. Attempt to use models that are no longer compatible with the installed extension.
5. Observe the HTTP 400 "model not supported" errors.
6. Manually update the Codex extension.
7. Retry the request.

**Observed result:** The original issue disappeared after updating the extension.

**Expected result:** Codex should identify outdated client compatibility as a possible cause and provide clear update guidance.


### What is the expected behavior?

_No response_

### Additional information

## Related issues

I found several existing reports that appear relevant:

- **#32412 — Codex IDE doesn't work with GPT 5.6 models**
  
  Particularly relevant because this also concerned an outdated IDE extension. The author confirmed that updating the extension resolved their issue.

- **#54422 — Windows app: outdated client offers unusable models without an update notice or actionable recovery guidance**
  
  Very similar symptoms and user experience, but affecting the Windows desktop application rather than the Linux VS Code extension.

- **#54234 — Codex Windows App: HTTP 400 – ChatGPT account not supported for any model**
  
  Documents the same misleading HTTP 400 error in the Windows client, with updating the application ultimately resolving the problem.

- **#53865 — List models that need a newer Codex as unavailable, with an "update Codex" reason, instead of hiding them**
  
  Proposes a closely related improvement to model compatibility information and update guidance.

I recognize that these issues concern different clients and may not all share the same underlying cause.

However, they illustrate a recurring usability problem: **outdated Codex clients can produce model availability or authentication errors without clearly identifying a required update as the solution**.

## Suggested improvement

A compatibility check at extension startup, or when a model request fails, could prevent considerable unnecessary troubleshooting.

For example:

> **Codex update may be required**
>
> Your installed Codex extension may be too old to use the currently available models.
>
> Please check for updates in VS Code's Extensions panel.
>
> If automatic updates are disabled, you may need to update the extension manually.

This would be particularly helpful for users who have disabled extension auto-updates, intentionally or otherwise.

items.title: Preserve rollout access metadata across compression and restoration
items.body:
Preserve rollout access metadata across compression and restoration

## Why

Replacing rollout files can lose Unix ownership or macOS ACLs, changing who can read or append to a transcript. An ACL can also permit appending while denying explicit timestamp updates.

## What changed

- Preserve Unix ownership, permissions, modification times, and macOS ACLs before publishing compressed or restored rollouts, and verify the replacement can be reopened.
- Abort replacement on metadata failures, reject macOS delete-deny ACLs to keep temporary files removable, and detect Unix access metadata changes through `ctime` checks.
- Use managed restoration temporary files whose names avoid stale `*.tmp` cleanup.
- Allow appending when refreshing the rollout's modification time returns `PermissionDenied`.

## Testing

Add regression coverage for macOS ACL preservation, inherited ACL removal, deletion-protected rollouts, append access despite denied timestamp changes, Unix group preservation, and restoration temporary files surviving stale-file cleanup.

items.body:
# [Desktop 0.163.0-alpha] Sending `reasoning.effort: "none"` for a model whose supported levels do not include `none`

**Environment**
- openai-codex-desktop (omarchy package) build `26.1013.40934-1`
- Bundled codex-cli `0.163.0-alpha.10.2` (system `codex-cli 0.163.0` also installed)
- OS: Linux x64, omarchy (Arch-based)
- Model in conversation: `gpt-6.1-sol`

**What happened**
A turn in a desktop conversation failed with a client-visible error banner:

```
Codex error event: Unsupported value: 'none' is not supported with the
'gpt-6.1-sol' model. Supported values are: 'low', 'medium', 'high',
'xhigh', and 'max'. (code=unsupported_value)
Dismissed when you send your next message.
```

`gpt-6.1-sol` has no `'none'` reasoning level anywhere in the model list
returned by the API (per `~/.codex/models_cache.json`, supported levels are
`low, medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra`). So the send layer constructed a
turn context with `reasoning.effort = "none"` that no available model can
accept.

**Investigation on my machine**
- `~/.codex/config.toml`: `model_reasoning_effort = "medium"`
- `state_5.sqlite` `threads` table for the affected threads: `model = "gpt-6.1-sol"`, `reasoning_effort = "medium"`
- Rollout JSONLs for the day: only `"effort":"medium"` occurrences
- Queue, session storage, app config: the string `"none"` appears nowhere as an effort value

Conclusion: the value was not read from any user-persisted setting. It was
injected at send time by the desktop app layer, apparently as a stale or
default per-chat reasoning state that drifted from the persisted value.

**Reproduction**
So far only observed on one conversation on an alpha desktop build. Steps
that appear to trigger it:
1. Start a desktop conversation against `gpt-6.1-sol`.
2. Let the per-chat reasoning picker state drift (hard to pin down; in my
   case the persisted state trusted by the DB was `medium` while the send
   layer attempted `none`).
3. Send a turn. The request is rejected with `code=unsupported_value`.

**Expected**
The send layer should never emit an effort value outside the model's
`supported_reasoning_levels`. If a persisted per-chat state references an
unsupported value, the app should clamp it to the closest supported level
(or surface a picker reset) instead of sending a request that is
guaranteed to be rejected.

**Actual**
The request is sent with `'none'`, the API rejects it, and the user sees
an error banner with no obvious way to know why or how to reset the chat
state.

**Workaround**
Starting a new chat, restarting the desktop app, or reselecting Medium in
the reasoning picker each clear the broken per-chat state. The terminal
CLI (`codex-cli 0.163.0`) does not reproduce because it sends effort
directly from `~/.codex/config.toml`.

items.title: Batch thread history materialization into SQLite
items.body:
Batch thread history materialization into SQLite

## Why

History catch-up collected the entire durable rollout prefix before applying it in one SQLite transaction. Large rollouts therefore required buffering all projection steps and committing them together.

## What changed

Stream projection batches through a bounded queue and commit each batch with its checkpoint. Flush between complete records after reaching 1 MiB of source data or 256 projection steps, keeping ordinal gaps with their following records and allowing oversized records to remain intact.

Wait for batches before opening SQLite transactions so an idle reader does not hold the writer. Preserve committed progress across later failures or cancellation, allowing retries to resume from the last checkpoint.

## Testing

Add coverage for reader and writer failures under backpressure, atomic batch rollback, retries without replaying committed records, and unrelated writes while projection is paused. Verify that producer disconnection and consumer cancellation retain committed progress.

items.body:
**Version:** codex-cli 0.162.1 (also seen on 0.156.1), `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`, launched through the npm `codex.js` wrapper.

**What happens.** A supervisor process (Node.js) runs `codex exec --json` and reads its stdout through a pipe. While it persists each chunk, the supervisor pauses reading. Sometimes Codex then exits with code 101:

```
thread 'codex-main' panicked at library/std/src/io/stdio.rs:1165:9:
failed printing to stdout: Resource temporarily unavailable (os error 11)
```

**Pattern (9 of 71 runs over 3 days).** Each panic comes right after Codex writes an `item.completed` event for a `command_execution` with a large `aggregated_output`. The JSON line is 31–65 KB, close to the 64 KiB pipe buffer. Runs without such large events do not crash. A retry of the same task usually succeeds.

**Why we think it happens.** `print!`/`println!` panic on any write error, including `WouldBlock`. A blocking write cannot return `EAGAIN`, so fd 1 has `O_NONBLOCK` set at that moment. We did not confirm which process in the chain sets it.

**Expected.** The JSONL writer should not panic on `EAGAIN`. It can wait for the fd to be writable and retry, or clear `O_NONBLOCK` on fd 1 at startup.

items.title: [Windows/MSIX] Browser is not available: iab - 3 root causes: MSIX EXDEV breaks Statsig identity, backend migration never fires (code-level), Cloudflare challenges on renderer API

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
## Environment

- OS: Windows 11 (MSIX packaged desktop app)
- App: OpenAI.Codex **26.1013.4894.2** (Developer-signed local build, previously Store 26.1013.4894.0)
- Bundled browser plugin: **26.1013.40934**
- Account: ChatGPT Plus
- Related issues: #47270, #52044, #43210, #45028, #53912

## Summary

On the Windows MSIX build, `agent.browsers.list()` only ever returns `Codex MCP Apps` (type `mcpapps`); `agent.browsers.get("iab")` always fails with `Browser is not available: iab`. After extensive local diagnosis I found **two stacked root causes**, one of which appears to be unreported so far.

## Root cause #1 (unreported): MSIX AppData virtualization EXDEV breaks Statsig identity

The official manifest declares `virtualization:ExcludedDirectories` with **only** `$(KnownFolder:LocalAppData)\OpenAI`. `%APPDATA%\Codex` (i.e. `RoamingAppData\Codex`) is **not** excluded, so the Electron renderer's writes under `C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\Codex\web\Codex\` are redirected by the MSIX VFS filter into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\OpenAI.Codex_*\LocalCache\Roaming\...`.

The VFS filter fails `rename()` on **dot-prefixed temp files** in that redirected directory. Desktop log evidence (host log under `LocalCache\Local\Codex\Logs`):

```
warning [global-state] Failed to persist global state errorCode=EXDEV
  errorMessage="EXDEV: cross-device link not permitted, rename
  'C:\Users\...\AppData\Roaming\Codex\web\Codex\.statsig-state.json.tmp-1792133428353-...'
  -> 'C:\Users\...\AppData\Roaming\Codex\web\Codex\statsig-state.json'"
warning [electron-message-handler] Failed to initialize host Statsig identity errorCode=EXDEV ...
```

Because `statsig-state.json` can never be persisted, the host Statsig identity never initializes 鈥?which plausibly cascades into abnormal `experimentalFeature` results and downstream feature gating.

**Fix that worked locally** (official-schema field, same pattern OpenAI already uses for `LocalAppData\OpenAI`): add a second entry to `virtualization:ExcludedDirectories`:

```xml
<virtualization:ExcludedDirectory>$(KnownFolder:RoamingAppData)\Codex</virtualization:ExcludedDirectory>
```

After repacking with that entry: `statsig-state.json` + `.bak` are written to the real `%APPDATA%\Codex\web\Codex\`, EXDEV occurrences drop to zero, and `browser_use_iab_backend_startup_ready backend=iab` begins firing. **Request: please add `$(KnownFolder:RoamingAppData)\Codex` to the shipped manifest's ExcludedDirectories.**

Note: `desktop6:FileSystemWriteVirtualization disabled` (already present in the manifest) only governs package-root writes 鈥?it does not affect AppData redirection, which is controlled solely by `virtualization:ExcludedDirectories`.

## Root cause #2 (matches #43210/#45028): IAB session route is a per-window singleton and gets disposed/stolen

Even with Statsig healthy, the host log shows a persistent imbalance on multi-session usage:

- `browser_use_iab_backend_startup_ready backend=iab` 鈥?19 occurrences
- `No ChatGPT browser route is available for browser session <id>` 鈥?**61 occurrences**

Reproduction pattern (timestamps correlate exactly):

```
11:40:08 IAB_LIFECYCLE rebound browser sidebar window owner...        (user opened a NEW chat)
11:40:10 IAB_LIFECYCLE created browser use host conversationId=client-new-thread:<new>
11:40:17 IAB_LIFECYCLE iab backend info request FAILED for the OLD session 01a13f26-...
          errorMessage="No ChatGPT browser route is available for browser session 01a13f26-..."
```

Any agent turn in a session that is not the currently-activated one fails `getInfo` 鈥?the route belongs to whichever session the sidebar owner currently points at. This matches #43210 ("backend started then route immediately disposed after stale completion") and #45028 ("route disappears after successful getInfo, persists after full app-data reset").

I deliberately did **not** patch `ensureBrowserUseSessionRoute` / `disposeBrowserUseRoute` in the bundled JS: changing the route lifecycle locally risks webview/renderer leaks (there is a known leak failure mode when CodexBrowser renderers are not released), so I'm asking for an official fix instead.

## Current state after local fixes

- EXDEV: 0; `Failed to initialize host Statsig identity`: 0
- `browser_use_iab_backend_startup_ready backend=iab`: fires for many sessions
- `browser_use_availability_resolved available=true browserPane=true reason=local-patched`
- But `agent.browsers.list()` still returns only `mcpapps` whenever the test session is not the active one; in a single-session, stay-on-the-session test the backend is ready but discovery/selection still needs verification.

## Minimal reproduction

1. Install any Windows MSIX build of Codex Desktop.
2. Open chat A, send a message, then open chat B (route moves to B).
3. While B is active, send a browser request in A (e.g. resume A and ask it to `agent.browsers.list()`).
4. A reports `Browser is not available: iab`; host log shows `No ChatGPT browser route is available for browser session <A>`.

## Addendum 2 (2026-10-19): code-level mechanism of the route-migration break

The bundled `main-C4DYk222.js` shows the backend binds to a temporary `client-new-thread:<uuid>` session at startup and is only migrated to the real conversation id via `moveBackendSession`, gated inside `canServeSession`:

```js
canServeSession(e, t) {
  let { sessionId: n } = t;
  if (this.backendStatesBySessionId.get(n) !== t) return false;
  if (e.conversationId === n) return this.ensureSessionRoute(e);
  if (this.pendingLocalWorkSessionIds.size !== 1
      || !this.pendingLocalWorkSessionIds.has(n)
      || this.sessionRoutes.has(e.conversationId)) return false;   // <-- dead-end
  let r = this.sessionRoutes.get(n);
  return r == null || this.delegate?.isWindowAlive(r.windowId) !== true ? false
    : (this.pendingLocalWorkSessionIds.delete(n),
       this.localWorkCodexSessionIds.set(n, e.conversationId),
       this.moveBackendSession(n, e.conversationId), ...)
}
```

Observed failure on 26.1013.4894.2 with a single fresh chat (session `01a153b9-...`), Cloudflare healthy, `browser_use_iab_backend_startup_ready backend=iab` fired, route captured for `client-new-thread:d652f0c6-...`:

- `agent.browsers.list()` 鈫?only `mcpapps` (its `metadata.codexSessionId` = the real conversation id)
- `get("iab"/"chrome"/"edge")` 鈫?`Browser is not available: <family>`
- Host log: **`moveBackendSession` never fires**; the `pendingLocalWorkSessionIds.size === 1` gate and/or the missing `sessionRoutes.has(realId)` state keeps `canServeSession` returning false, so `list_browsers` never includes any family entry for the session.

This is the concrete mechanism behind #43210/#45028: the `client-new-thread` 鈫?real-conversation backend migration is fragile (needs exactly one pending backend, window alive, no pre-existing route for the real id). Any session switching, extra new chats, or timing skew permanently strands the backend.

## Addendum (2026-10-19 later): third stacked layer 鈥?Cloudflare challenges on ALL renderer API calls

After fixing #1 above and observing #2, the host log shows the renderer's chatgpt.com fetches are being **mass-challenged by Cloudflare** 鈥?62 + 41 occurrences per app session on two different exit IPs (both datacenter ranges):

```
sa_server_request_failed errorCode=cloudflare_challenge status=403
  url=/settings/user, /models, /conversations, /pins,
  /aip/first-party/eligibility,   <-- first-party eligibility check
  /celsius/ws/user, /automations, /amphora/notifications ...
chatgpt_pubsub_connection_failed errorMessage=cloudflare_challenge
```

- `/aip/first-party/eligibility` returning 403 means the first-party eligibility check cannot complete 鈥?plausibly gating iab discovery on top of #2.
- Switching exit IPs (two different datacenter ranges) did not help, while the same IP works fine for the regular Chrome browser against chatgpt.com 鈥?so this looks like a Cloudflare rule targeting the Codex desktop renderer's request signature, intermittently, rather than a pure IP-reputation issue.
- Cross-reference: openai/codex#50579 and BigPizzaV3/CodexPlusPlus#2407 (multiple users, intermittent, "fixed itself after a few hours" / "re-selecting the workspace in Settings then retrying helped").

Community-reported mitigations for the CF layer (unverified by me yet): re-select / reinstall the workspace in Settings 鈫?retry; wait for server-side rule to clear (intermittent).

## Requested fixes

1. Add `$(KnownFolder:RoamingAppData)\Codex` to the shipped manifest `virtualization:ExcludedDirectories` (fixes EXDEV / Statsig identity on MSIX).
2. Fix the IAB route lifecycle so a session's route survives session switching / stale completion events, or at minimum re-capture on demand in `ensureBrowserUseSessionRoute` instead of throwing.
